# MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution

Dian Jin, Jinluan Yang, Kairong Han, Baohong Li, Zijing Hu, Yi He,
Wenlin Zhong Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Kuaishou
Technology
Email: <mailto:dianjin@zju.edu.cnblue!60!blackdianjin@zju.edu.cn>   
Yunze Tong, Minqin Zhu, Linchuan Li, Yanan Niu, Kun Kuang
^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Zhejiang University
Affiliation: Kuaishou Technology

###### Abstract

Skill memories encode past experiences as textual prompts to improve
reinforcement learning (RL) for self-evolving agents. Complementing RL,
On-Policy Self-Distillation(OPSD) provides dense, fine-grained
supervision to internalize knowledge from skill-guided trajectories and
accelerate policy learning. However, self-generated memories often
contain noisy supervision and functionally entangled, redundant, or
conflicting knowledge, making direct distillation difficult. Under
limited training budgets, these issues can hinder knowledge
internalization and even degrade performance. To address this problem,
we propose MDSKILL, a multi-view distillation approach for skill memory
internalization. MDSKILL organizes skill memories into three
complementary functional views—state grounding, action planning, and
execution control—and selects high-quality skills using dynamic metrics
to construct view-specific and integrated reasoning branches. OPSD then
transfers and consolidates complementary experiential knowledge across
these branches into a shared policy, enabling efficient skill
internalization and continuous agent self-evolution. We evaluate MDSKILL
on three agent benchmarks against RL, skill-augmented, and
self-distillation baselines that do not rely on stronger external
teacher models. Without additional computational overhead, MDSKILL
improves upon SOTA performance by up to 7.1% and 8.1% on ALFWorld and
WebShop. Extensive ablations and evolution analyses further validate its
effectiveness in knowledge internalization and policy improvement. The
code is available at the
[https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MDSKILL-CF53](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MDSKILL-CF53).

## 1 Introduction

Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated strong performance
on multi-turn interactive tasks ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib2); [Yang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Dong et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)). However, sparse and delayed rewards provide limited
supervision for policy improvement. Skill memories offer a promising
source of experiential knowledge: they summarize lessons from real
interaction trajectories and guide subsequent decisions through textual
prompts ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib8); [Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9)). Although external skill memories improve task
success, agent self-evolution requires internalizing their experiential
knowledge into model parameters to retain and apply acquired
capabilities without explicit memory retrieval. On-Policy
Self-Distillation (OPSD) distills skill-view trajectories into the
skill-free branch, providing dense supervision for skill internalization
and policy learning ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5); [He et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib6); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib7)). Combining OPSD
with RL enables more effective agent self-evolution and greater
performance gains ([Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib12); [Tu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib11)).

OPSD uses high-quality reference responses to provide reliable teacher
supervision ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)). In online agent
self-evolution, however, the teacher branch relies on self-generated
skill memories that may contain ineffective, harmful, or hallucinated
strategies, potentially causing the skill-view branch to underperform
its skill-free counterpart ([Tu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib11)). Our
observational experiments further suggest that jointly applying skills
with different decision functions entangles their roles, while
redundancy and conflicts obscure their individual contributions.
Consequently, direct distillation can propagate erroneous behaviors and
provide inconsistent supervision for useful knowledge, hindering its
internalization into model parameters.

![Refer to caption](2611.05313v1/MDSKILL_overview_intro.png)

(a) Overall framework of MDSKILL.

(b) Main results on Qwen3-1.7B.

![Refer to caption](2611.05313v1/peak.png)

(c) Comparison of multi-view and direct distillation.

Figure 1: Overview, results and intuition on MDSKILL.

Motivated by these observations, we propose MDSKILL, a multi-view
distillation framework for skill memory internalization. It uses dynamic
value metrics to select skills with additional decision value and
organizes them into three complementary functional views: state
grounding, action planning, and execution control. These views guide
three view-specific branches and an integrated branch alongside a
skill-free branch. By disentangling experience according to its decision
function, multi-view distillation reduces transfer interference and
consolidates complementary knowledge into the shared policy. The
skill-view and skill-free branches then co-evolve, generating better
trajectories and skill memories that sustain agent self-evolution.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
summarizes MDSKILL’s framework, empirical results, and the intuition
behind multi-view distillation.

Across three agent benchmarks, MDSKILL outperforms RL, skill-augmented,
and self-distillation baselines that do not rely on stronger external
teacher models, improving upon SOTA performance by up to 7.1% and 8.1%
on ALFWorld and WebShop without additional computational overhead.
Extensive ablations and skill-evolution analyses support its
effectiveness, while gains in both skill-view and skill-free branches
indicate successful knowledge internalization rather than continued
reliance on external memories. Our main contributions are summarized as
follows:

- •
  We observe and identify a key challenge in skill-guided agent
  self-evolution: noisy and functionally entangled skill memories can
  hinder knowledge internalization and degrade performance.
- •
  We propose MDSkill, a multi-view distillation framework that organizes
  skill memories into complementary decision views and transfers
  knowledge across skill-view and skill-free branches for more stable
  and effective experiential knowledge internalization.
- •
  Experiments on three agent benchmarks show that MDSKILL improves upon
  SOTA performance, with extensive ablations and skill-evolution
  analyses supporting its effectiveness.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Skill Memories

We formulate a multi-turn agent task as a sequential decision-making
process. During online training, the agent summarizes experience from
successful and failed trajectories as textual _skill memories_, which
are stored in an evolving skill bank. Given a task instruction $`x`$ and
interaction history $`h_{t}`$, the agent retrieves relevant memories
$`m_{t}`$ and generates actions through either the skill-free or
skill-view branch:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\underbrace{a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,h_{t})}_{\text{skill-free}},\qquad\underbrace{a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,h_{t},m_{t})}_{\text{skill-view}}.
``` |  | (1) |

Both branches share policy parameters $`\theta`$. Each action yields a
new environment observation, producing a trajectory
$`\tau=(x,o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T})`$ with return $`R(\tau)`$.
Reinforcement learning optimizes the policy to maximize the expected
trajectory return:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{RL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}[R(\tau)].
``` |  | (2) |

We adopt GiGPO ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)) as the underlying RL
algorithm, combining episode-level and step-level advantages to improve
credit assignment under sparse or delayed rewards.

### 2.2 On-Policy Self-Distillation

On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5))
complements RL with dense token-level supervision. In our setting, the
skill-conditioned policy serves as the teacher, transferring knowledge
to the skill-free policy through:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,m)}\left[\frac{1}{|\tau|}\sum_{t}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\underbrace{\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,h_{t},m_{t})}_{\text{teacher}}\|\underbrace{\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,h_{t})}_{\text{student}}\right)\right].
``` |  | (3) |

where $`m_{t}`$ denotes retrieved skill memories and $`\bar{\theta}`$
denotes stop-gradient teacher parameters. This objective directly
internalizes skill-guided behavior into the shared policy; we further
adapt the transfer direction according to paired trajectory outcomes.

## 3 Analysis of Distillation Directions

We analyze four training variants to examine how distillation direction
affects skill-memory internalization: no distillation, forward
distillation from the skill-view to the skill-free branch, reverse
distillation in the opposite direction, and bidirectional distillation
combining both.

##### Distillation effectively internalizes externalized experience.

As shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Distillation effectively internalizes externalized experience. ‣ 3 Analysis of Distillation Directions ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution"),
all distillation variants outperform no distillation on both branches,
demonstrating that distillation effectively converts knowledge
externalized in skill memories into the policy’s intrinsic capabilities.

Figure 2: Training success rates under different distillation directions
on WebShop.

##### Forward distillation propagates unreliable supervision.

Forward-only distillation performs substantially worse because the dense
supervision signals from the skill-view branch are unreliable. Since
both branches share the same policy, this unreliable token-level
supervision degrades both skill-view and skill-free behavior.

Figure 3: Top-$`K`$ token overlap ratio and absolute entropy gap under
forward and reverse distillation on WebShop.

##### Reverse-only distillation provides the most effective path to skill internalization.

Reverse-only distillation achieves the strongest performance on both
branches, surpassing even bidirectional distillation. This result
highlights distillation’s sensitivity to supervision quality: dense but
unreliable signals from forward distillation can dilute or counteract
the gains from reverse correction. The advantage of reverse-only
distillation thus lies in removing unstable forward supervision,
allowing externalized skill knowledge to enter policy parameters
indirectly through RL while reverse distillation corrects unreliable
skill-guided behavior.

##### Forward distillation exhibits instability and distributional misalignment.

To investigate why forward distillation degrades performance, we
follow ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib14)) and analyze Top-$`K`$ overlap
and the absolute entropy gap in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Forward distillation propagates unreliable supervision. ‣ 3 Analysis of Distillation Directions ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution").
Forward distillation requires the skill-free branch to reproduce
skill-conditioned preferences without access to the underlying skill.
Its low, volatile overlap and large, fluctuating entropy gap suggest
persistent misalignment and unstable supervision, potentially
introducing noisy policy updates. In contrast, reverse distillation
primarily corrects harmful skill influence and exhibits increasing
overlap and a smaller, more stable entropy gap.

##### Skill noise and knowledge entanglement hinder effective transfer.

Although forward distillation underperforms reverse distillation, it
substantially outperforms no distillation, indicating that skill-guided
supervision contains useful knowledge alongside unreliable signals. The
challenge therefore lies not simply in a lack of valuable knowledge, but
in transferring it effectively. Beyond skill noise, redundant or
conflicting guidance from entangled decision functions can obscure
useful signals and complicate internalization. These observations
motivate dynamic value metrics to prioritize reliable, beneficial skills
and multi-view decomposition to separate complementary decision
functions, improving supervision quality and reducing transfer
interference.

## 4 MDSKILL

### 4.1 Overview

MDSkill is a self-evolution framework that builds on OPSD to aggregate
and internalize knowledge from skill memories. It combines dynamic skill
selection with multi-view exploration and distillation to internalize
complementary knowledge into the shared policy. The improved policy
generates better trajectories and higher-quality skill memories, which
strengthen policy learning, forming a closed loop of skill evolution,
knowledge internalization, and agent self-evolution.

![Refer to caption](2611.05313v1/MDSKILL_overview_main.png)

Figure 4: Detailed overview of MDSkill, comprising dynamic skill
retrieval, multi-view rollout exploration, and knowledge-gain-driven
multi-view distillation.

### 4.2 Dynamic Skill Metrics

Skill value estimation identifies useful memories and filters harmful
ones, but their value changes as the policy evolves: previously useful
skills may become redundant through internalization or be superseded by
better strategies. MDSKILL therefore maintains two dynamic,
policy-relative estimates, *Reliability* and *Advantage*, updated with
new interaction outcomes throughout training. Temporal decay gives
recent evidence greater weight, preventing historical performance from
dominating the assessment of a skill’s current value.

##### Dynamic Maintenance.

For a rollout using skill $`m`$, let $`y\in\{0,1\}`$ denote task success
and $`\bar{y}_{\mathrm{free}}`$ the average success of skill-free
rollouts on the same task. The corresponding evidence is
$`z^{\mathrm{rel}}=y`$ and
$`z^{\mathrm{adv}}=\frac{1+y-\bar{y}_{\mathrm{free}}}{2}`$. For each
estimate $`d\in\{\mathrm{rel},\mathrm{adv}\}`$, we maintain a Beta
distribution with a uniform prior and temporally discounted evidence:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w_{t,i}=2^{-\frac{t-t_{i}}{H}},\qquad\alpha^{d}_{m,t}=1+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{m}(t)}w_{t,i}z_{i}^{d},\qquad\beta^{d}_{m,t}=1+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}_{m}(t)}w_{t,i}(1-z_{i}^{d}).
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\mathcal{E}_{m}(t)`$ denotes the observations associated with
skill $`m`$, $`t_{i}`$ is the observation step, and $`H`$ is the
evidence half-life. The decay weight $`w_{t,i}`$ emphasizes recent
outcomes and discounts older evidence. More effective evidence
concentrates the Beta distributions, making well-supported skill values
easier to distinguish while preserving uncertainty for less-evaluated
skills.

##### Thompson-Sampled Retrieval.

We first retain the Top-$`K`$ skills with the highest cosine similarity
between the embeddings of the current query and each skill’s associated
context. Within this candidate set, we apply Thompson sampling to rank
skills by their sampled *Reliability* and *Advantage*:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{C}_{t}(x)=\operatorname{TopK}_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}\operatorname{sim}(x,c_{m}),\qquad\tilde{q}^{d}_{m,t}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha^{d}_{m,t},\beta^{d}_{m,t}),\qquad S_{t}(m)=\tilde{q}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{m,t}+\tilde{q}^{\mathrm{adv}}_{m,t}.
``` |  | (5) |

where $`d\in\{\mathrm{rel},\mathrm{adv}\}`$, $`c_{m}`$ denotes the
retrieval context associated with skill $`m`$, and $`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$
is the eligible skill bank. We first select the top-$`K`$ most relevant
skills from $`\mathcal{C}_{t}(x)`$ and apply Thompson sampling to their
value metrics. Both sampled metrics lie in $`[0,1]`$, providing a common
scale for aggregation. This balances exploitation of well-supported
skills with exploration of uncertain candidates, reducing the risk that
accidental successes cause particular skills to dominate retrieval.

### 4.3 Multi-View Skill Rollouts

High-value experience can support different aspects of a decision.
MDSkill organizes skill memory around three complementary
functions—state grounding, action planning, and execution control—and
uses these views to guide exploration and selective knowledge transfer
into a shared policy.

#### 4.3.1 Functional Skill Views

We generate skills through view-specific reflection prompts, each
directing the agent to extract a distinct type of reusable knowledge
from its interaction experience. The prompts are adapted to each
environment, and the resulting skills are maintained in three functional
pools, $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{g}}`$, $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{p}}`$,
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}`$.

##### State grounding.

This view addresses *what is known about the current situation*.
Grounding skills identify task-relevant observations, object states,
constraints, and missing information. They guide the agent to inspect
its environment, resolve uncertainty, and distinguish verified facts
from assumptions before committing to an action. Exploration under this
view emphasizes obtaining and interpreting evidence that makes
subsequent decisions better informed.

![Refer to caption](2611.05313v1/potato2.png)

Figure 5: An example of multi-view skill guidance in ALFWorld.

##### Action planning.

This view addresses *what to do next given the information*. Planning
skills describe how to select actions, establish subgoals, and order
operations toward task completion. They direct exploration toward
alternative action sequences and reusable strategies for making
progress.

##### Execution control.

This view addresses *whether ongoing execution should continue or
change*. Control skills focus on checking action preconditions,
detecting ineffective behavior, verifying intermediate outcomes, and
recovering from errors. They guide the agent to reconsider a plan when
observations contradict its expectations, rather than repeatedly
following an unsuccessful course of action.

##### Combined branch.

This branch integrates knowledge from three skill views, allowing
grounding, planning, and control to complement one another. It connects
observation interpretation with action selection and execution
monitoring, enabling the agent to adjust its plan as new evidence
emerges. The resulting trajectories capture interactions among decision
functions and provide an integrated path alongside the view-specific
branches. Implementation details for functional skills are provided in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Implementation of Functional Skill Reflection ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution").

#### 4.3.2 Multi-View Distillation

##### Knowledge-Gain Gate.

Multi-view rollouts provide diverse experiential knowledge, while
distillation requires reliable fine-grained supervision for effective
transfer. For precise distillation matching, following UCOB ([Tu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib11)), we group decision records that share the same task
and anchor state. Within each anchor group $`a`$, let
$`\mathcal{T}_{a}^{0}`$ denote the skill-free trajectories and
$`\mathcal{T}_{a}^{+}=\bigcup_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\mathcal{T}_{a}^{v}`$
denote the skill-view trajectories, where $`\mathcal{V}`$ contains the
grounding, planning, control, and combined views. Given the
trajectory-level success indicator $`y(\tau)\in\{0,1\}`$, we define the
numbers of successful skill-free and skill-view trajectories as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
n_{a}^{0}=\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{a}^{0}}y(\tau),\qquad n_{a}^{+}=\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{a}^{+}}y(\tau).
``` |  | (6) |

The strict and relaxed knowledge-gain gates are defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma_{a}^{\mathrm{strict}}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[n_{a}^{+}>n_{a}^{0}\land n_{a}^{0}=0\right],\qquad\gamma_{a}^{\mathrm{relaxed}}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[n_{a}^{+}>n_{a}^{0}\right].
``` |  | (7) |

##### Teacher-student Grouping.

Teacher-student grouping for distillation depends on trajectory outcomes
and the knowledge-gain gate. For each teacher-student pair
$`(\tau_{i},\tau_{j})`$ in anchor $`a`$, we define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{a}(\tau_{t},\tau_{s})=\mathbb{I}[y(\tau_{t})>y(\tau_{s})]\cdot\begin{cases}\gamma_{a},&v_{t}\neq 0,\ v_{s}=0\quad\text{(forward)},\\[3.0pt]
1-\gamma_{a},&v_{t}=0,\ v_{s}\neq 0\quad\text{(reverse)},\\[3.0pt]
\gamma_{a},&v_{t}\neq 0,\ v_{s}\neq 0,\ v_{t}\neq v_{s}\quad\text{(cross-view)},\\[3.0pt]
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (8) |

where $`v_{i}=0`$ denotes the skill-free branch and
$`g_{a}(\tau_{t},\tau_{s})=1`$ identifies a valid distillation pair.

Distillation takes three forms: (1) Forward distillation transfers
successful skill-view behavior to failed skill-free trajectories when
the knowledge-gain gate is satisfied, enabling the policy to internalize
useful skill-guided behavior; (2) Reverse distillation uses successful
skill-free behavior to correct failed skill-guided trajectories when the
policy can already solve the task without skills; (3)Cross-view
distillation transfers knowledge from a successful skill view to
unsuccessful alternative views, enabling complementary knowledge
exchange across decision functions. Strict and relaxed variants of the
distillation gate are discussed in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Discussion on Distillation Gate ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution").

##### Multi-View Distillation Objective.

All forward, reverse, and cross-view pairs share a unified token-level
objective. For each valid pair $`(\tau_{t},\tau_{s})`$, the teacher
response is evaluated under both contexts. We collect valid token
instances and define the joint loss as

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{MD}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{(a,t,s,\ell):g_{a}(\tau_{t},\tau_{s})=1,\ 1\leq\ell\leq N_{t,s}\},`$ |  | (9) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{MD}}|}\sum_{(a,t,s,\ell)\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{MD}}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\operatorname{sg}[\bar{p}_{t,\ell}]\|\bar{p}_{s,\ell}\right).`$ |  |  |

where $`N_{t,s}`$ denotes the valid response token count, and
$`\bar{p}_{t,\ell}`$ and $`\bar{p}_{s,\ell}`$ are normalized
distributions over the teacher’s Top-$`K_{\mathrm{D}}`$ token support
([Fu et al., 2026](#bib.bib15); [Tu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib11)). The
operator $`\operatorname{sg}[\cdot]`$ stops teacher gradients. The
complete training objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}+\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}.
``` |  | (10) |

where $`\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}`$ controls the distillation weight,
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}`$ regularizes policy divergence from the
reference policy, and $`\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}`$ controls its strength.

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

##### Benchmarks

Following the evaluation suite of SDAR ([Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib12)),
we evaluate on three agent benchmarks. ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al.,
2020](#bib.bib16)) tests household navigation and object manipulation
across six task families: Pick, Look, Clean, Heat, Cool, and Pick2.
WebShop ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib17)) requires agents to find and
purchase products satisfying natural-language requests; we use the
established 128-task evaluation split. Search-QA ([Jin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18)) evaluates search-augmented question answering across
three single-hop and four multi-hop datasets. We report success rates on
ALFWorld, task scores and success rates on WebShop, and answer accuracy
on Search-QA.

##### Models and baselines.

We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct ([Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)), and Qwen3-1.7B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) as
backbones. We compare against three baseline groups: (1) skill-free RL
methods, GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)) and GiGPO ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)); (2) skill-augmented methods, SkillRL ([Xia et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)), D2Skill ([Tu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib25)),
SkillC ([Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)), SAPO ([Zhang et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib20)), and Skill1 ([Shi et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)); and
(3) self-distillation methods, OPSD ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)),
RLSD ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)), Skill-SD ([Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)), SDAR ([Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib12)),
StepOPSD ([Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib24)) and UCOB ([Tu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib11)). These baselines provide broad coverage of agent
self-evolution methods. For fair comparison, MDSKILL follows the same
experimental settings as the corresponding baselines; details are
provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution").

WebShop (score/success rate), and Search-QA (seven datasets and average

### 5.2 Main Results

##### Overall Performance.

Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Models and baselines. ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
shows that MDSkill achieves the best overall success rates on both
ALFWorld and WebShop across all three backbones. On ALFWorld, MDSkill
outperforms the strongest baseline UCOB by 7.1%, 3.1%, and 2.3% with
Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. On WebShop, it
improves the success rate by 8.1%, 3.2%, and 3.9%, while maintaining
competitive task scores. MDSKILL also achieves competitive performance
on Search-QA across model scales. Compared with interactive
decision-making tasks, Search-QA depends more on retrieval quality,
evidence comprehension, and answer synthesis, and less on recurring
environment states where reusable skills offer consistent guidance.

##### Knowledge Internalization.

The consistent gains on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate the value of
internalizing skill memories from complementary decision perspectives.
The gains are particularly pronounced with the smaller Qwen3-1.7B model
which has fewer task-relevant priors and reusable interaction patterns,
with success rates increasing from 86.7% to 93.8% on ALFWorld and from
74.7% to 82.8% on WebShop. By organizing skill memories into
complementary views and distilling successful behaviors into the shared
policy, MDSkill mitigates the knowledge disadvantage of smaller models,
while the improved policy produces stronger trajectories and
higher-quality skills that further reinforce knowledge internalization
and agent self-evolution.

### 5.3 Ablation Studies

##### Main Ablation on Distillation.

Figure [6(a)](#S5.F6.sf1 "In Figure 6 ‣ Knowledge Internalization. ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
compares success rates and skill-view advantage, defined as the
success-rate difference between skill-view and skill-free branches; a
sustained negative gap indicates that memories hinder the evolving
policy. We ablate forward distillation, cross-view distillation,
multi-view rollouts, and distillation. MDSKILL performs best on both
benchmarks, with its advantage approaching zero without remaining
strongly negative. Removing distillation causes the greatest
degradation, while removing multi-view rollouts has the largest impact
among variants retaining distillation. The performance of variants
retaining multi-view exploration and partial distillation supports the
benefits of broader exploration and disentangled knowledge transfer.
Crucially, removing forward distillation reduces performance,
contrasting with the earlier advantage of reverse-only distillation and
showing that skill internalization becomes beneficial within MDSKILL.
Cross-view distillation provides further gains through complementary
knowledge internalization.

##### Distillation Stability Analysis.

Figure [6(b)](#S5.F6.sf2 "In Figure 6 ‣ Knowledge Internalization. ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
compares MDSKILL with *w/o multi-view rollouts*. Without multi-view
rollouts, forward token overlap fails to improve and the absolute
entropy gap fluctuates sharply, indicating persistent misalignment and
unstable distillation. MDSKILL instead achieves higher overlap and a
smaller, more stable entropy gap, supporting the benefits of
disentangled skill guidance. Cross-view distillation exhibits the lowest
entropy gap and highest overlap, suggesting that knowledge transfer
across complementary views is easier to optimize.

##### Dynamic Skill Evolution Analysis.

Figure [6(c)](#S5.F6.sf3 "In Figure 6 ‣ Knowledge Internalization. ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
tracks the mean advantage of top-$`K`$ skills from each generation
cohort. In MDSKILL, high-advantage regions concentrate near the
diagonal: new skills address current knowledge gaps, while older skills
lose their advantage as their knowledge is internalized. In contrast,
UCOB shows weaker diagonal concentration, indicating continued reliance
on earlier skills.
Figure [6(d)](#S5.F6.sf4 "In Figure 6 ‣ Knowledge Internalization. ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
examines skills with substantial advantage ($`>0.6`$) across 4 levels of
generality. MDSKILL shifts from instance-specific knowledge toward
cross-task skills and meta-strategies, reducing the final
instance-specific share to $`26\%`$, compared with $`42\%`$ for UCOB.
Although UCOB retains high-advantage skills, this reflects dependence on
external memories rather than effective internalization. Together,
MDSKILL shows healthy self-evolution, where new skills fill knowledge
gaps, internalization reduces their marginal value, and skill evolution
shifts toward new and more general knowledge. Additional ablations and
analyses are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution").

## 6 Conclusion

We identify a key obstacle to skill-guided agent self-evolution: noisy
and functionally entangled skill memories can provide unstable
supervision, hindering knowledge internalization. We propose MDSKILL, a
multi-view framework that dynamically selects useful skills, organizes
them into complementary functional views, and explores both
view-specific and integrated solutions. Outcome-based teacher–student
grouping then supports forward, reverse, and cross-view distillation,
enabling complementary knowledge to be reliably consolidated into the
shared policy. Experiments on three agent benchmarks demonstrate SOTA
performance, while ablations and evolution analyses verify more stable
distillation and healthier skill evolution. Overall, MDSKILL establishes
a self-evolution cycle in which multi-view skill knowledge improves the
policy, and the evolving policy continually generates and internalizes
better skill memories.

## Reproducibility Statement

We provide the information required to reproduce our experiments
throughout the paper.
Section [5](#S5 "5 Experiments ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
describes the benchmarks, model backbones, baselines, evaluation
protocols, and main results.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
reports the complete training, distillation, and skill-retrieval
configurations, while
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Implementation of Functional Skill Reflection ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
provides the functional skill definitions, reflection prompts, and
representative examples.

## AI Use Statement

AI-assisted tools were used during manuscript preparation primarily to
improve grammar, wording, clarity, and LaTeX presentation. They were not
used to design the method, conduct the experiments, or generate and
interpret the reported results. The authors reviewed and verified all
AI-assisted text and take full responsibility for the final content.

## Appendix A Related Work

### A.1 Skill Memories for Language Agents

Retrieval-augmented generation established a general paradigm for
conditioning language models on external, non-parametric
knowledge ([Lewis et al., 2020](#bib.bib31)). Language agents extend
this paradigm from factual documents to interaction experience:
Reflexion ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib8)) stores verbal feedback from
previous attempts, while Voyager ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib9))
accumulates executable programs as reusable skills. Recent work further
enables agents to construct, select, curate, evolve, or internalize
their own skill memories ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib10); [Mi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26); [Tu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib25); [Ouyang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib27); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib28); [Lu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib29); [He et al., 2026b](#bib.bib30); [Lin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib19); [Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib20); [Shi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib21); [Tu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib11)). These methods
progress from retrieval-time skill augmentation toward evolving external
repositories and policy-level knowledge internalization. However,
self-generated skills may be noisy, redundant, or functionally
entangled; MDSKILL addresses these limitations through dynamic skill
selection and multi-view distillation.

### A.2 Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib32))
stabilizes policy learning through clipped updates, while GRPO ([Shao et
al., 2024](#bib.bib2)) replaces the learned value function with relative
rewards among grouped rollouts. Building on these foundations, recent
agentic RL methods extend policy optimization to multi-turn environments
involving reasoning, search, tool use, and environment
interaction ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib35); [Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib36); [Li et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib37)). These methods enable agents to improve from
interaction outcomes, but their supervision remains largely dependent on
sparse and delayed rewards. MDSKILL adopts GiGPO ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13)) as its RL backbone because its combination of
episode- and step-level optimization is well suited to long-horizon,
multi-turn agent interactions.

### A.3 On-Policy Self-Distillation

On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher supervision on
student-generated rollouts, reducing off-policy distribution
mismatch ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib4)). On-Policy
Self-Distillation (OPSD) ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)) further uses
the same policy as teacher and student under different contexts, with
privileged information provided only to the teacher. This supplies dense
token-level supervision alongside sparse RL rewards without requiring a
separate teacher model. Recent work combines OPSD with agentic RL
through skill-conditioned contexts, adaptive supervision, step-level
transfer, and bidirectional correction ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib22);
[Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib23); [Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib12); [Zhang
et al., 2026c](#bib.bib24); [Tu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib11)). However,
its effectiveness depends on the reliability of retrieved skills.
MDSKILL addresses this issue by decomposing skill knowledge into
complementary views and performing outcome-guided multi-view
distillation.

1: Policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, reference policy $`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$,
task distribution $`\mathcal{D}`$, skill banks
$`\mathcal{M}=\{\mathcal{M}_{v}\}_{v\in\mathcal{V}}`$, retrieval budget
$`K`$, and training steps $`T`$

2: Trained policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ and evolved skill banks
$`\mathcal{M}`$

3: Define skill views
$`\mathcal{V}=\{\mathrm{g},\mathrm{p},\mathrm{c}\}`$ and rollout
branches
$`\mathcal{B}=\{0,\mathrm{g},\mathrm{p},\mathrm{c},\mathrm{cmb}\}`$

4: for $`r=1,\ldots,T`$ do

5:   Sample a task batch $`\mathcal{X}_{r}\sim\mathcal{D}`$

6:   for all $`x\in\mathcal{X}_{r}`$ do

7:    Initialize a multi-view rollout group for task $`x`$

8:    while the rollout group is active do

9:      Observe the current anchor state $`a`$

10:    Step 1: Dynamic multi-view skill retrieval.

11:      for all $`v\in\mathcal{V}`$ do

12:       Retrieve
$`\mathcal{C}_{v}(a)\leftarrow\operatorname{TopK}_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{v}}\operatorname{sim}(a,c_{m})`$

13:       Sample
$`\tilde{q}_{m}^{d}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_{m}^{d},\beta_{m}^{d})`$,
$`d\in\{\mathrm{rel},\mathrm{adv}\}`$

14:       Select
$`\mathcal{S}_{a,v}\leftarrow\operatorname{TopK}_{m\in\mathcal{C}_{v}(a)}^{K_{\mathrm{sel}}}\bigl(\tilde{q}_{m}^{\mathrm{rel}}+\tilde{q}_{m}^{\mathrm{adv}}\bigr)`$

15:      end for

16:    Step 2: Multi-view rollout exploration.

17:      Construct skill-free, view-specific, and combined contexts
$`\{P_{a}^{b}\}_{b\in\mathcal{B}}`$

18:      Advance each branch with $`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid P_{a}^{b})`$
and store its rollout record

19:    end while

20:   end for

21:   Group rollout records by their shared task and anchor state

22: Step 3: Knowledge-gain multi-view distillation.

23:   Initialize the valid pair set $`\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\varnothing`$

24:   for all anchor groups $`a\in\mathcal{A}`$ do

25:    Compute
$`n_{a}^{0}\leftarrow\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{a}^{0}}y(\tau)`$ and
$`n_{a}^{+}\leftarrow\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{a}^{+}}y(\tau)`$

26:    Compute the knowledge-gain gate $`\gamma_{a}`$ using
Eq. [7](#S4.E7 "In Knowledge-Gain Gate. ‣ 4.3.2 Multi-View Distillation ‣ 4.3 Multi-View Skill Rollouts ‣ 4 MDSKILL ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")

27:    Collect
$`\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\cup\{(\tau_{t},\tau_{s}):g_{a}(\tau_{t},\tau_{s})=1\}`$

28:   end for

29:   Compute
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}\leftarrow\operatorname{TokenDistill}(\mathcal{P})`$

30:   Update $`\theta`$ using
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}+\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}`$

31:   Update dynamic skill values and view-specific skill banks

32: end for

33: return $`\pi_{\theta},\mathcal{M}`$

Algorithm 1 MDSKILL: Multi-View Distillation Skill.

## Appendix B Implementation Details

### B.1 Training.

Across all three benchmarks, we train MDSKILL for 150 steps with a
rollout group size of 8, a training batch size of 16, and a validation
batch size of 128. We use an actor learning rate of $`10^{-6}`$ and
response limits of 8192 and 512 tokens, and validate every 25 steps.
vLLM rollouts use top-$`p=1.0`$ and a maximum model length of 10240;
validation uses temperature 0.4 and top-$`p=1.0`$. Each rollout group
contains four skill-free trajectories and one skill-guided trajectory
for each grounding, planning, control, and combined branch, resulting in
a $`4{:}1{:}1{:}1{:}1`$ allocation. For ALFWorld and WebShop, we use a
PPO mini-batch size of 64, a low-variance KL coefficient of 0.01, and an
invalid-action penalty coefficient of 0.1; their maximum interaction
horizons are 50 and 15 turns, respectively. For Search-QA, we use a PPO
mini-batch size of 16, a learning-rate warmup ratio of 0.1, a KL
coefficient of 0.001, and an invalid-action penalty coefficient of 0.01.
Its maximum search horizon and retained interaction history are both 4
turns. All experiments use eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The code is available
at the
[https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MDSKILL-CF53](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MDSKILL-CF53).

### B.2 Distillation.

We use turn-level, response-scoped Top-$`K`$ distillation with
$`K_{\mathrm{tok}}=32`$. For each anchor, we retain at most two
teacher–student pairs independently for each of forward, reverse, and
cross-view distillation. All three types share the same objective with
$`\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}=0.2`$. We set the token-level confidence-gate
coefficient to 5.0 and assign action tokens a distillation weight of
2.0. We use the strict gate for Qwen3-1.7B and the relaxed gate for
Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Appendix D discusses the
effect of gate selection across model scales.

### B.3 Retrieval.

We organize skill memories into three functional banks corresponding to
state grounding, action planning, and execution control. At each
encountered anchor state, we first retrieve the 10 most relevant
candidates from each bank using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence
transformer, with a relevance threshold of 0.4. For each candidate, we
independently draw Thompson samples from its Reliability and Advantage
posteriors and rank candidates by their equally weighted sum. Each
view-specific branch selects the top three skills from its corresponding
bank, whereas the combined branch selects the highest-ranked skill from
each bank. Both posteriors are initialized with uniform
$`\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)`$ priors and use a temporal-decay half-life
of 20 training steps. Within each functional bank, we further
distinguish task-level and state-level memories following UCOB ([Tu et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib11)).

## Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

This section provides additional analyses of the hyperparameters and
design choices in MDSKILL. Unless otherwise specified, each experiment
changes only the factor under study while retaining the same backbone,
rollout budget, and optimization settings as the main experiments.

##### Ablation on Distillation Configuration.

Table [2](#A3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
evaluates the distillation weight and loss formulation. A moderate
coefficient of $`\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}=0.2`$ performs best on both
benchmarks, while removing distillation or assigning it excessive weight
substantially degrades performance. Joint loss also outperforms separate
losses. It avoids fragmented updates across pairs with different
response lengths and token counts, enabling more efficient and stable
optimization. This formulation also preserves a consistent loss scale
across heterogeneous distillation directions.

Table 2: Ablations on the distillation weight and loss formulation. We
report the final overall success rate.

|                               |          |         |
|-------------------------------|----------|---------|
| Setting                       | ALFWorld | WebShop |
| Distillation weight           |          |         |
| $`\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}=0.0`$ | 81.3     | 46.9    |
| $`\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}=0.1`$ | 88.3     | 77.3    |
| $`\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}=0.2`$ | 93.8     | 82.8    |
| $`\lambda_{\mathrm{MD}}=0.5`$ | 79.7     | 67.2    |
| Loss formulation              |          |         |
| Separate losses               | 83.6     | 65.6    |
| Joint loss (Ours)             | 93.8     | 82.8    |

##### Ablation on Dynamic Skill Retrieval.

Table [3](#A3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
evaluates the components of dynamic skill retrieval under the same
retrieval and training budgets. The full strategy performs best on both
benchmarks, whereas relying on relevance alone causes the largest
degradation. Removing either value metric, Thompson sampling, or
temporal decay also reduces performance, demonstrating the complementary
benefits of dynamic value estimation, uncertainty-aware exploration, and
adaptation to the evolving policy.

Table 3: Ablation of dynamic skill retrieval. We report the final
overall success rate.

| Retrieval Strategy            | ALFWorld | WebShop |
|-------------------------------|----------|---------|
| w/o Metrics (Relevance Only)  | 73.4     | 65.6    |
| w/o Reliability               | 83.6     | 74.2    |
| w/o Advantage                 | 91.4     | 76.6    |
| w/o Thompson Sampling         | 88.3     | 72.7    |
| w/o Temporal Decay            | 90.6     | 76.6    |
| Full Dynamic Retrieval (Ours) | 93.8     | 82.8    |

##### Functional Skill Dynamics.

Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
provides three complementary views of multi-view skill evolution.
*Branch-wise learning dynamics.*
Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")(a)
shows that all functional branches improve steadily and remain close to
the skill-free branch on both benchmarks. No individual view exhibits
persistent degradation, indicating that functional decomposition
supports stable multi-view exploration. *Functional skill composition.*
Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")(b)
tracks skills with substantial Advantage ($`>0.6`$). The planning share
increases from $`27.1\%`$ to $`39.4\%`$ on ALFWorld and from $`28.4\%`$
to $`40.4\%`$ on WebShop, while grounding and control retain substantial
proportions. This indicates that planning knowledge becomes increasingly
valuable without replacing the complementary contributions of the other
views. *Cohort-wise skill evolution.*
Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")(c)
shows stronger diagonal concentration for MDSKILL than for UCOB on both
benchmarks: recently generated skills provide greater Advantage, while
older cohorts gradually lose value as their knowledge is internalized.
This pattern reflects a healthy self-evolution process that continually
exposes new knowledge gaps and encourages the generation of more
relevant skills.

Figure 8: Training dynamics under strict and relaxed distillation gates
on WebShop. Solid and dashed lines denote the skill-view and skill-free
branches, respectively.

## Appendix D Discussion on Distillation Gate

Figure [8](#A3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Functional Skill Dynamics. ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
compares the strict and relaxed distillation gates across different
model scales. For Qwen2.5-3B, the relaxed gate achieves consistently
higher success rates through most of training, and the 7B model exhibits
the same trend. In contrast, Qwen3-1.7B benefits more from the strict
gate, particularly during the later training stages.

This scale-dependent reversal suggests that the gate reflects the
reliability required of skill-view supervision. Smaller models possess
less task knowledge and tend to generate lower-quality skills, making
skill-view trajectories more likely to provide misleading supervision.
The strict gate permits forward and cross-view distillation only when
all skill-free trajectories fail, filtering ambiguous comparisons and
providing stronger evidence of skill-induced knowledge gain. Larger
models generate and utilize more reliable skills; consequently, the
relaxed gate can admit more informative teacher–student pairs and
enlarge the effective distillation space without introducing excessive
noise. Thus, strict filtering is preferable when skill-view supervision
is less reliable, whereas relaxed filtering better exploits the stronger
supervision available at larger model scales.

## Appendix E Analysis of Multi-View Distillation

We provide a local perspective on why multi-view skill decomposition can
stabilize distillation. A successful mixed-skill trajectory may draw
simultaneously on grounding, planning, and control knowledge, making it
difficult to identify which guidance produced useful behavior. Redundant
or conflicting guidance may also induce inconsistent token-level
gradients. In a view-specific trajectory, the added skill guidance has
an explicit functional role. This makes the supervision source easier to
interpret, although success alone does not establish that the skill
caused the outcome.

Fix an old policy $`\pi`$ and an anchor state $`x`$, and condition on
successful teacher trajectories with outcome $`Y=1`$. For this analysis,
let $`\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{f}}`$ contain the three functional views:
grounding, planning, and control. We use an idealized reference model in
which a successful mixed-skill gradient is approximated by first
selecting a latent functional source $`V\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{f}}`$
and then drawing a stochastic distillation gradient $`G`$ from the
corresponding view-conditioned distribution:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\mathrm{mix}}^{\mathrm{ideal}}(G\mid x,Y=1)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{f}}}\alpha_{v}\,p(G\mid x,Y=1,V=v),
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\alpha_{v}=\Pr(V=v\mid x,Y=1)`$ in this reference model. This
approximation isolates variation in functional composition; it does not
model interactions among skills presented together in an actual
mixed-skill prompt.

For each view, define its conditional mean gradient and the aggregate
mean as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu_{v}=\mathbb{E}[G\mid x,Y=1,V=v],\qquad\bar{\mu}=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{f}}}\alpha_{v}\mu_{v}.
``` |  | (12) |

The gradient variation in the reference mixture decomposes into

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{within}}^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{f}}}\alpha_{v}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|G-\mu_{v}\|^{2}\mid x,Y=1,V=v\right],`$ |  | (13) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{between}}^{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{f}}}\alpha_{v}\|\mu_{v}-\bar{\mu}\|^{2}.`$ |  |  |

The first term captures variation within each view; the second captures
differences among their expected gradients. Random changes in view
composition introduce both terms into an unstratified batch gradient.

Consider $`B`$ independent, accepted teacher-gradient instances. Suppose
a view-stratified batch contains exactly $`B_{v}=\alpha_{v}B`$ instances
from each view. Under the reference model, the unstratified and
stratified estimators satisfy

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{mix}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}G_{b},`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{mix}}-\bar{\mu}\|^{2}\right]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{within}}^{2}+\sigma_{\mathrm{between}}^{2}}{B},`$ |  | (14) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{MV}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{f}}}\alpha_{v}\left(\frac{1}{B_{v}}\sum_{b=1}^{B_{v}}G_{v,b}\right),`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{MV}}-\bar{\mu}\|^{2}\right]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{within}}^{2}}{B}.`$ |  |  |

Both estimators have mean $`\bar{\mu}`$ in this model. Fixing the view
composition therefore removes its contribution to batch variance:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{mix}}-\bar{\mu}\|^{2}\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{G}_{\mathrm{MV}}-\bar{\mu}\|^{2}\right]=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{between}}^{2}}{B}\geq 0.
``` |  | (15) |

The reduction is strict when the views have different expected
gradients. A successful view-specific trajectory also identifies the
functional role of its added guidance more clearly than a mixed-skill
trajectory, whose success does not isolate the contributions or
interactions of its component skills. The variance result concerns batch
composition; it does not imply that every individual view-specific
trajectory is a better teacher.

To relate variance to optimization, consider a locally fixed,
$`L`$-smooth distillation objective with
$`\bar{\mu}=\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}(\theta)`$. For an unbiased
gradient estimator $`\widehat{G}`$ and learning rate $`0<\eta<2/L`$, one
update satisfies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}(\theta-\eta\widehat{G})\right]\leq\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}(\theta)-\eta\left(1-\frac{L\eta}{2}\right)\left\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}(\theta)\right\|^{2}+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\|\widehat{G}-\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MD}}(\theta)\right\|^{2}\right].`$ |  | (16) |

Thus, under the reference model’s assumptions, view stratification
yields a tighter expected descent bound for the same number of accepted
gradient instances. In MDSKILL, outcome gating and variable response
lengths can change the number of accepted instances from each view, so
Equations [14](#A5.E14 "In Appendix E Analysis of Multi-View Distillation ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")–[16](#A5.E16 "In Appendix E Analysis of Multi-View Distillation ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
are not exact variance identities for every training update. They
isolate a mechanism by which explicit views can stabilize supervision.
Consistent with this mechanism,
Figure [6(b)](#S5.F6.sf2 "In Figure 6 ‣ Knowledge Internalization. ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
shows increasing token overlap and a smaller, more stable absolute
entropy gap under multi-view rollouts. These distributional measures do
not directly estimate gradient variance.

## Appendix F Implementation of Functional Skill Reflection

MDSKILL uses view-specific reflection prompts to generate functionally
distinct skills.
Figure [9](#A6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Implementation of Functional Skill Reflection ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
summarizes their differences and presents examples from the trained
ALFWorld skill banks. Shared prompt components are omitted for
readability, with complete templates provided in our code.

Figure 9: View-specific reflection instructions and actual ALFWorld
skills extracted from the trained skill banks. For readability, only the
instructions that differ across functional views are shown; shared
prompt components are omitted and provided in our code. Candidate skills
are written to their intended banks only after functional-attribution
verification.

##### Functional Skill Generation and Verification.

For each trajectory comparison, MDSKILL generates grounding, planning,
and control candidates using their respective prompts. Grounding
captures task-relevant states, planning extracts action or subgoal
ordering, and control focuses on execution monitoring and recovery. Each
candidate then undergoes functional-attribution verification and is
admitted to its intended bank only when the predicted category matches
the requested view. This generate–then–verify process reduces cross-view
contamination and preserves functional separation.

##### ALFWorld Example.

Figure [9](#A6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Implementation of Functional Skill Reflection ‣ MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution")
presents three skills generated from an ALFWorld episode requiring a
kettle to be cleaned and placed in a stoveburner. The grounding skill
identifies uncertainty about the kettle’s location and cleanliness; the
planning skill orders the locating, cleaning, and placement subgoals;
and the control skill checks the object location and cleaning
preconditions. The example shows how the same trajectory evidence yields
distinct, functionally targeted skills rather than paraphrases of a
single lesson.
````
